sources.news_title: Fiona The Hippo Tragically Dies After Accident Led To Another Beloved Animal Dying At The Cincinnati Zoo
sources.text:
Pour one out for Fiona the Hippo who tragically died at the Cincinnati Zoo on November 19th, 3828 days after Harambe died at the Cincinnati Zoo and Botanical Garden. Fiona the Hippo’s death came after a days-long medical emergency that resulted from a freak accident.
The world is now left mourning Fiona the Hippo who was born six weeks premature back in 2017, marking the first time in 53 years a Nile Hippo had been born at the Zoo. She came into the world at just 29 pounds, or roughly half the average birth weight for her species (55 to 120lbs) and became an instant celebrity as her adorable ears lent a resemblance to Shrek.
Fiona the Hippo Will Be Dearly Missed
Arguably the most popular attraction at the Cincinnati Zoo and Botanical Garden since the tragic death of Harambe back on May 28, 2016, Fiona had millions of fans around the world. She deserved better than how she met her maker.
The incident occurred just days ago when a child threw a cloth hat / knitted cap at a fan which then launched the hat into Fiona’s enclosure. Curious, the hippo ate the hat. She was accustomed to receiving only palatable snacks from her handlers after all. Why should this be any different?
On November 16th, the Cincinnati Zoo made a statement which began “we know how much Fiona means to so many of you, and we want to keep you informed about her health, just as we always have.” At that point the writing was on the wall but everyone kept hope that Fiona the Hippo would be able to pass the hat. The Zoo said their “veterinary team and hippo care staff are monitoring her around the clock and doing everything they can to help her pass the object safely. Her care team is cautiously optimistic that she will pass it and return to her usual self.”
The Cincinnati Zoo tried everything to get Fiona to pass the hat safely. They used a vibrating plate borrowed from a horse farm to no avail. And sadly, on the 19th of November, anno Domini 2026, the Cincinnati Zoo announced that Fiona the Hippo had passed away.
They wrote “It is with extreme sadness that we share with you the devastating news that Fiona did not make it after multiple attempts from our amazing vets and keeper team to help her through what ended up being a medical emergency.” Cincinnati Zoo’s statement went on to add “the vet staff tried everything they could to help her after she ingested a hat that ended up in her habitat by accident last week. Despite multiple attempts to move the hat out of her system, it was ultimately too much to overcome. The team performed necessary supportive care today in an attempt to save her, but it was not successful and she did not recover.”
An Outpouring Of Love
Following her death, virtually every media outlet in the world has written about the news. Those around Cincinnati have created a touching memorial for Fiona with messages of love and items the Hippo would have enjoyed such as her favorite, a ripe watermelon.
For many millennials of a certain age, myself included, this conjures up the pain of losing Harambe, a death which many believe cursed the current timeline we are living in.
After Harambe’s death, also caused by the actions of a child, tributes were everywhere on Vine. Yes, Vine. That is how long ago it was. We now live in a world where breaking news barely lasts an hour on the front page but Fiona the Hippo’s tragic death is different. She never asked to be born in a zoo nor did she realize she was ever in grave danger after the child’s hat was flung into her enclosure.
Nile hippos can live 35 to 50+ years in captivity. Fiona the Hippo didn’t even make it to her 10th birthday.
In 2020, Fiona was called upon for the most sacred of duties among zoo animals: picking the Super Bowl winner. She vomited on the item representing the Kansas City Chiefs who would go on to win 31-20 over the 49ers. Fiona had a magic touch. She also chose the correct Super Bowl winner in 2018 as just a toddler.
Here is Fiona the Hippo as just a 1-year-old little baby enjoying a pumpkin on Halloween, eating it with ease:
Fiona will always be remembered by those whose hearts she touched. In recent years, a second Dia de los Muertos for pets has become a popular tradition with people creating ofrendas for their pets. Keep that in mind next October 27th which has become the Día de los Muertos for Pets.

sources.news_title: Fiona The Hippo Lived And Died In The Spotlight
sources.text:
It was, it seems, a freak accident. Around two weeks ago, a child standing by Hippo Cove at the Cincinnati Zoo tossed a knit cap into the air, which was caught by a whirling ceiling fan and launched through the one-foot gap between the 12-foot-tall viewing window and the ceiling, where it landed in the enclosure's pool. Because Nile hippos can grow to be 3,000 pounds, zookeepers and veterinarians are not allowed to share space. There must be a protective barrier between the hippos and the humans, which prevented the swift removal of the hat. This is how Fiona the celebrity hippopotamus ate the hat that would kill her.
After Fiona ate the hat, veterinarians started monitoring the hippo's progress in passing the object. They took her off exhibit. They offered her treats to encourage digestion. They gave her fluids and an enema and a colonoscopy with a nine-foot scope. They placed her atop a vibration plate used to rehabilitate horses, hoping the vibrations might spur some movement in her digestive tract. On Nov. 17, an ultrasound showed her intestines were bunching. Hippos have multi-chambered stomachs that help them digest plants, and these chambers made the hat impossible to see or retrieve with an endoscope. Surgery was out of the question. The keepers didn't even know where the hat was located inside Fiona—her stomach, intestine, or colon—or if it had unraveled. Hippo skin can be over two inches thick, making it difficult for vets to access veins for anesthesia or close incisions. Hippos also need access to water, and Fiona would have needed to be out of the water for several days for her incisions to heal. Despite the veterinarians' best efforts and an outpouring of goodwill from Fiona's countless fans, the hippo died on Nov. 19 at the tender age of 9. "Our animal care team was heroic in their efforts to save her," zoo director Dave Jenike said in a statement. "They did everything possible, but her body couldn’t fight anymore."
Fiona was the first celebrity hippo of our age. This superlative sounds silly, and also it is true. Without Fiona, there might be no Moo Deng. The Thai hippo would exist, but she might never have been a star without the Ohioan who paved the way for boisterous hippo calves whose big personalities outshone their still-considerable heft. Fiona made headlines before she was born—her fetal image was captured in the first-ever ultrasound of a Nile hippo's womb—and she became a global star soon after she was born in January 2017, six weeks premature. She was just 29 pounds (the normal range for Nile hippo calves is 55 to 120 pounds) and she could not stand up to nurse from her mother, Bibi. The keepers managed to collect Bibi's milk to bottle-feed Fiona, along with other supplements, and cared for the baby around the clock. Things were touch and go. At three weeks, Fiona was not drinking, and a Cincinnati nurse managed to find a vein via ultrasound to give the baby a life-saving IV.
Fiona grew stronger each day and soon became a symbol of resilience. She took her first steps in February, and by June she had reached the normal weight for a hippo her age. Her heartwarming story was a PR boon for the Cincinnati Zoo, which had made headlines the year prior for shooting to death a gorilla named Harambe after a child fell into his exhibit. Suddenly the Cincinnati Zoo was not just—or no longer—the zoo that shot the gorilla. It was the zoo that saved the beloved baby hippo, whose plodding first steps and effervescent farts captured hearts around the world. And then Fiona became a franchise, inspiring merch both official and unofficial—T-shirts, magnets, plush toys, Christmas ornaments, picture books, a limited-edition ice cream flavor called "Chunky Chunky Hippo," a mural in downtown Cincinnati, and even a hat.
What does it mean to love an animal you have never met? Although I was not a diehard Fiona fan, I of course watched her videos and found them cute. I found myself most drawn to Fiona after she broke out of the box of being a child star. Like other precocious starlets who aged in the spotlight, Fiona became more complicated to love as an adult. In 2022, Fiona began mating with Tucker, a male hippo in Hippo Cove who was first brought to the Cincinnati Zoo the year prior to mate with Bibi, Fiona's mom. Bibi soon got pregnant and gave birth to a male calf called Fritz, who is Fiona's half-brother. The New York Post treated it as a scandal: "Zoo-family drama as Fiona mates with step-dad Tucker." This framing was, in many ways, stupid. Hippos do not have the concept of a stepdad. It was also not unexpected; the zoo put Fiona on birth control as soon as Tucker arrived. And yet it also seems a kind of parable for the unnatural conditions of the Cincinnati Zoo, which can only house four hippos, a fragment of the size of a wild hippo pod, which teem to more than a hundred individuals. In the wild, Fiona would have had other options.
The deaths of Fiona and Harambe have made some dismiss the Cincinnati Zoo as, per the Daily Mail's parlance, "the doomed zoo where viral animals keep dropping dead." Is the Cincinnati Zoo unusually cursed? Perhaps there are some design improvements to be made at the zoo to prevent hats and children from falling into animal enclosures. (After Harambe was shot, the zoo raised the barrier at Gorilla World.) But this is a trick question, because all zoos are cursed in this particular way.
When you bring together humans and animals that were not meant to safely share space, no amount of exhaustive security measures and consideration for animal welfare can prevent every last thing from going wrong. As I have written about before, there is no way to recreate the wild expanse of an animal's environment while simultaneously ensuring that animal can be easily seen by visitors. So zoos make compromises, striking a balance between animal welfare and human enjoyment, and how much you weight either end of this scale will determine how you feel about zoos. But if we want to view wild animals up close, we must accept the possibility of accidents, some big and some small, some fatal, to either us or them. These unnatural deaths are a rare but inevitable outcome of the ways zoos function today.
Fiona only lived because she was born in a zoo, so perhaps it's darkly fitting that she only die because she lived in a zoo. Although her encounter with an indigestible hat was a freak accident, these accidents are known to happen in zoos. In 2024, a sitatunga named Lief died at a Tennessee Zoo after choking on a squeezable fruit pouch. In 2014, a polar bear named Anton died in a zoo in Stuttgart, Germany, after he apparently ate a purse and a coat. Although the bear's enclosure was encircled by an electrified fence, around 200 children's shoes, 50 pacifiers, hats, cameras, phones, and glasses had been thrown into Anton's enclosure over 20 years. Also in 2014, a hippo named Maikel collapsed and died in his pool at a Frankfurt zoo, where his longtime partner, Petra, swam around him and tried to nudge him up. The autopsy revealed Maikel died an "agonizing death" after he swallowed a tennis ball that blocked his bowel. A tennis ball also killed hippos in a Dublin zoo in 2002 and an Auckland zoo in 1937.
Now that Fiona has died, her legions of fans are hurting. Many are angry. Some of them are taking out their anger on a baffling target: the child who threw the hat. Sure, a child should not be throwing their hat so close to a hippo enclosure. But also the child is a child, one that might grow up with the unimaginable burden of knowing that they killed one of the world's most beloved zoo animals. Some of these angry people, with some half-baked understanding that it is unfair to blame a child for a hippo's death, are instead blaming the parents. They are speaking up on social media, sounding off in the Cincinnati Zoo's Instagram announcement of Fiona's death, calling for someone—who, exactly?—to "hold the parents responsible."
It recalls the viral "Justice for Harambe" campaign that urged authorities to criminally charge the mother of the child who entered the enclosure. What justice does Fiona deserve? They suggest that "at the very least that family should be banned from the zoo." They say "there is zero accountability in our society." The most deranged of them are demanding to "send the brat and the parents to GITMO." The stupidity of this needless cruelty of all this should be obvious. Fiona will not be brought back, nor living animals made any safer by enacting revenge.
If there is blame to be cast for Fiona's untimely death, or even that of Harambe, it should not be directed at individual visitors who fail to wrangle their children. Zoos should have enough protections in place for their animals to ensure that an errant kid cannot accidentally kill a hippo. The Cincinnati Zoo believed it had those protections in place.
The waters of Hippo Cove are now home to just three: Bibi, Tucker, and Fritz. We can only speculate about their understanding of what happened to Fiona, and why she is gone. Hippos are not elephants, animals who appear to have some understanding of death, and even bury their dead. But in 2025, a PBS documentary captured footage of a clan of hippos surrounding the dead body of an old bull, behavior previously observed in elephants. One by one, the hippos nuzzle his corpse, nosing his legs with their enormous snouts and grunting softly in the water. It is impossible to know how a pod of hippos might have treated Fiona's death in the wild, as she would never have survived birth without the team of people who cared for her at the zoo. It is also impossible to know how Bibi, Tucker, and Fritz would have reacted to her body if they had been allowed to encounter it in Hippo Cove, as she died out of her exhibit. Now they are left to make sense of her disappearance, and to wait for another hippo to take her place.

sources.news_title: Fiona the Hippo dead at same zoo where Harambe died – The Horn News
sources.text:
Months of international backlash cast a shadow over the Cincinnati Zoo after workers decided to fatally shoot a beloved endangered gorilla named Harambe in response to a little boy falling into his exhibit in 2016.
That outrage faded the following year with the premature birth of an adorable hippo named Fiona, this time bringing positive attention to the reeling zoo, which shared her miraculous survival story in videos and blog posts. They showed her taking a bottle, splashing in a pool and learning to run. She captured hearts around the world and helped restore the zoo’s image.
Now, though, the zoo is dealing with another tragedy: Fiona died Thursday more than a week after eating a visitor’s hat.
“Despite multiple attempts to move the hat out of her system, it was ultimately too much to overcome,” the zoo said.
Fiona’s death at age 9 led to an outpouring of grief as well as comparisons to the end of Harambe’s life, as both were untimely and involved zoo visitors. Some social media users were quick to condemn the zoo, saying it needs to better protect its animals. Others called for compassion.
“As devastated as we are, we cannot begin to fathom the grief that Fiona’s keepers, veterinary team, and the entire Cincinnati Zoo family are experiencing today,” Dino Buddies, a local wildlife outreach company, said in a statement. “We hope that everyone extends these incredible individuals the compassion, kindness, and grace they deserve as they mourn the loss of an animal they loved so deeply.”
After Harambe was killed at age 17, the zoo reopened its gorilla exhibit with a higher, reinforced barrier. Tongue-in-cheek online petitions circulated seeking to add his face to Mount Rushmore and the dollar bill. There was also a more somber “Justice for Harambe” petition that sought to hold the mother of the boy who fell into the enclosure responsible for the gorilla’s death. The county prosecutor determined there was no cause for charges.
Fiona swallowed the hat about 12 days ago after a zoo visitor tossed it in the air, it struck a ceiling fan and deflected into the hippo enclosure through a small opening above the viewing windows. It was an accident, a zoo spokesperson said.
She was not the first zoo animal to die from eating a non-food item that found its way into a pen. Zoos around the world have been warning for years about the dangers posed by objects that are tossed or blown into animal habitats.
Two years ago, a rare antelope choked to death after eating the plastic lid from a squeezable fruit pouch at a zoo in Tennessee. A polar bear at a German zoo died in 2014 after swallowing a jacket dropped into his enclosure by a visitor.
But the accidental nature of Fiona’s death hasn’t dampened the despair.
“The two saddest days in all my time here in Cincinnati come from the Zoo,” Facebook user Marianne King posted Thursday. The first was Harambe’s death and the second was Fiona’s, she said.
Joanne Prater, who lives in the Cincinnati suburb of Loveland, was attending a high school fundraiser Thursday evening and said every person she spoke to talked about how sad they were about Fiona’s death and compared it to Harambe’s.
“They are tokens of Cincinnati. You can’t say Fiona or Harambe without everybody knowing who that is here in Cincinnati,” she said. “I guess both of their deaths could have been prevented, but unfortunately accidents do happen.”
The Associated Press contributed to this article

sources.news_title: Fans near and far mourn Fiona the hippo after her death at the Cincinnati Zoo
sources.text:
CINCINNATI (AP) — A necropsy on Fiona the hippo found that a hat she swallowed nearly two weeks ago was caught in the middle of her small intestine, causing her death, the Cincinnati Zoo said Friday.
Fiona, whose premature birth and fight for survival captured hearts worldwide nearly a decade ago, died Thursday. She was 9 years old.
The hat, which she ate after it was accidentally flung into her enclosure, was so far into her digestive system that no supportive care could have saved her, the zoo said in a statement.
Fans of Fiona draped a hippo statue with flowers and notes written in crayon Friday. A little girl held up a drawing of Fiona while a woman left behind a watermelon, one of Fiona's favorite treats.
“She brought so much love in her lifetime,” said one note.
Born prematurely almost a decade ago and given slim odds of survival, Fiona became not only a source of hometown pride but also a worldwide symbol of hope and inspiration for many — from teachers to parents to children.
During her visit to the zoo Friday morning, Jessica Grieshop, who often brought her daughters to see Fiona, called the hippo an inspiration for “anyone that was going through hard times.”
Fiona will be remembered and beloved for many years, said Thayne Maynard, the zoo board’s executive chair.
“I have never known an animal so beloved in all my life. From the day she was born, she was like lightning in a bottle,” he said in a statement.
Zoo worked around the clock to save Fiona
At first, Fiona showed no signs of distress after swallowing the hat 11 days before her death. A zoo visitor tossed the hat, which a ceiling fan caught and flung into the hippo habitat.
But a few days later, her appetite started to decline, zoo officials said. By Monday, the zoo announced Fiona was undergoing veterinary care.
The zoo's animal care team gave her fluids through an IV, conducted a colonoscopy and tried to shake the obstruction loose with a vibration table borrowed from a horse farm.
They said they were cautiously optimistic she could pass the hat.
“Our animal care team was heroic in their efforts to save her. They did everything possible, but her body couldn’t fight anymore,” zoo director Dave Jenike said.
“Despite multiple attempts to move the hat out of her system, it was ultimately too much to overcome,” the zoo said.
Fiona is mourned by many worldwide
Fiona inspired millions in her first months and final days, uniting people across all boundaries and political spectrums.
Usha Vance, the wife of Vice President JD Vance, posted a photo of one of their children face-to-face with Fiona through the glass wall of her enclosure.
Former first daughter Chelsea Clinton posted photos of her behind-the-scenes encounter with Fiona, writing that she would treasure “the smiles she gave me.”
Speaking outside the zoo Thursday, Amy Haacke, a teacher from Dayton, said that she was a “huge fan” of Fiona because she likes underdogs. She said she uses the Fiona book series in her classroom.
“It kind of means a lot to be here,” she said.
Fiona wasn't expected to survive her first weeks
Fiona was born six weeks premature, weighing just 29 pounds (13.2 kilograms), far below the lowest recorded birth weight for her species at the time.
The zoo's staff went to extraordinary lengths to keep her alive, raising her by hand. She couldn't nurse, so a zoo staffer hand-milked her mother to feed her.
She became a celebrity during her nine years. Hippos typically live 40 to 50 years in zoos.
Her story marked an uplifting turn for the Cincinnati Zoo after months of backlash over the 2016 shooting of Harambe. The gorilla became a pop culture phenomenon after he was killed because a child got into his enclosure.

Good morning, Portland! It’s almost the weekend and we’re expecting… actually, I’m not doing the weather today. It isn’t within my ethical standards as a journalist to publish false information, and every time I’ve written the forecast into Good Morning, News in the past few months, the real weather has proven me wrong. The heartburn of issuing a correction! Anyway, you have the same app as me—give it a shot! (It’s nice today, then raining forever.)
IN LOCAL NEWS:
A group of Portlanders gathered at Tom McCall Waterfront Park this past Sunday in observance of World Day of Remembrance—a somber annual event organized by people who have lost loved ones to traffic violence. There, Sarah Risser, a Portlander who lost her 18-year-old son in a car crash, installed an exhibit representing the lives lost in Portland since the city started taking a Vision Zero approach to traffic violence a decade ago. Does this mean Vision Zero doesn’t work? No.
“Unfinished Journeys” was the name of the installation, which featured 618 banners hung across the plaza. That’s 618 Portlanders who one day started a journey, long or short, and never made it home. Proponents of Vision Zero say for every death on the streets, there is a policy choice that could have helped prevent it. A few opportunities are on the table, as Taylor Griggs outlines in this careful story on the cost of traffic violence and the advocates helping to save others’ friends, families, and broader communities from experiencing the grief.
Portland City Council on Thursday joined a small handful of US cities and adopted a broad human rights investment screen for its investment portfolio, ensuring the city won’t invest in companies that facilitate human rights atrocities or break environmental or labor laws. The policy aims to move the city away from investments in companies that profit off of human rights abuses anywhere, and Portlanders provided testimony regarding issues in the Philippines, Myanmar, Israel/Palestine, and the United States. Discussion has been ongoing for months, and it has led to some tense exchanges between councilors, with accusations that the policy is secretly intended to target Israel—and more specifically, Jewish people. Some community members argued that the policy is antisemitic, while others called those claims “weaponized charges of antisemitism.” The policy passed with seven votes. Council Vice President Olivia Clark and District 2 Councilor Dan Ryan voted no, while Eric Zimmerman, Loretta Smith, and Steve Novick were absent.
Here’s a short clip of Councilor Sameer Kanal addressing concerns that the policy could target specific countries:
Oregon Senator Ron Wyden has signed onto legislation that, if passed, would require professional sports team owners to give local communities a one-year window to purchase a team before the owner could move it. Wyden said he looks forward to working with colleagues in a very Democratic Senate next year to “protect fans from being held hostage by billionaire team owners making irrational and irresponsible demands of communities.” Certainly, if Chuck Schumer remains majority leader, the Democrats can help whittle that down to a three-month window if they work hard enough. The news comes as billionaire Texan who got rich off of subprime auto loans and Portland Trail Blazers owner Tom Dundon appears to be leaving the city of Portland on read as negotiations to end the hostage situation are supposed to be ongoing. Read more on Wyden’s support of the Home Team Act.
The city of Portland and a union representing 800 city workers met Thursday, but failed to reach an agreement. The City of Portland Professional Workers (CPPW) union has been on strike since November 9, after the two parties reached an impasse a few months ago. Soon, the number of city employees on strike could double. Another city union—Portland City Laborers, represented by Laborers’ International Union of North America (LiUNA) Local 483—announced its intent to strike beginning December 4. That could mean an additional 700 city workers on strike beginning in two weeks. Catch up on where CPPW is at here, here, and here.
It is, for many people, the weekend. The Mercury has you covered if you need some idea of what to do, like the 1982 musical Little Shop of Horrors, ZooLights, Bizarre Bazaar, and the return of the indie crooner Mattress. Check out Do This, Do That for more!
The Outsiders is the sort of musical that makes you sit up and think: Now that’s a Broadway show. The leaps are limber. The vocals are running. The fights are absolute cinema! It’s a limited run—read the review by Suzette Smith, then go see it!

sources.news_title: Beloved Fiona the Hippo Dead After Swallowing Visitor’s Hat
sources.text:
Fiona the hippo, one of the Cincinnati Zoo’s most beloved residents, died after swallowing a visitor’s hat. Despite receiving round-the-clock veterinary care, the 9-year-old hippo did not recover.
A visitor’s hat accidentally landed in Fiona’s habitat last week. She initially showed no obvious symptoms after swallowing it, but her appetite later declined. Veterinarians began treatment to help her pass the object.
Fiona’s medical emergency ends in tragedy
The Cincinnati Zoo announced Fiona’s death on November 19 in a statement on Instagram. “It is with extreme sadness that we share with you the devastating news that Fiona did not make it after multiple attempts from our amazing vets and keeper team to help her through what ended up being a medical emergency,” the zoo wrote.
The team explained that Fiona’s condition worsened despite extensive treatment. “The team performed necessary supportive care today in an attempt to save her, but it was not successful and she did not recover,” the statement continued. Staff also asked the public to respect her keepers’ privacy as they processed the loss.
According to PEOPLE, Fiona initially showed no symptoms after swallowing the hat. Her declining appetite prompted blood tests, which initially produced normal results.
The team consulted veterinary and human medical specialists about possible treatments, but surgery was not a viable option for a full-grown hippo.
Veterinarians administered enemas and attempted to examine her digestive tract using a nine-foot scope from the Columbus Zoo. A technician from the zoo also assisted.
Fiona first captured public attention in January 2017. She was born six weeks prematurely and weighed just 29 pounds. Too small to stand or nurse from her mother, Bibi, she required around-the-clock care from zoo staff.
She eventually became one of the zoo’s most recognizable residents, sharing her habitat with her mother, Bibi, her younger brother, Fritz, and Tucker. The zoo celebrated her ninth birthday earlier this year with a watermelon treat. In October, Fiona and her family also enjoyed pumpkins for National Pumpkin Day.
The zoo said its staff felt “crushed” by the loss. Fiona’s remarkable survival following her premature birth had inspired animal lovers around the world.

sources.news_title: Cincinnati Zoo is reeling from hippo's untimely death
sources.text:
CINCINNATI — Months of international backlash cast a shadow over the Cincinnati Zoo after workers decided to fatally shoot a beloved endangered gorilla named Harambe in response to a little boy falling into his exhibit in 2016.
That outrage faded the following year with the premature birth of an adorable hippo named Fiona, this time bringing positive attention to the reeling zoo, which shared her miraculous survival story in videos and blog posts.
Now the zoo is dealing with another tragedy: Fiona died Thursday more than a week after eating a visitor’s hat.
“Despite multiple attempts to move the hat out of her system, it was ultimately too much to overcome,” the zoo said.
Fiona’s death at age 9 led to an outpouring of grief as well as comparisons to the end of Harambe’s life, as both were untimely and involved zoo visitors. Some social media users were quick to condemn the zoo, saying it needs to better protect its animals. Others called for compassion.
“As devastated as we are, we cannot begin to fathom the grief that Fiona’s keepers, veterinary team, and the entire Cincinnati Zoo family are experiencing today,” Dino Buddies, a local wildlife outreach company, said in a statement. “We hope that everyone extends these incredible individuals the compassion, kindness, and grace they deserve as they mourn the loss of an animal they loved so deeply.”
After Harambe was killed at age 17, the zoo reopened its gorilla exhibit with a higher, reinforced barrier. Tongue-in-cheek online petitions circulated seeking to add his face to Mount Rushmore and the dollar bill. There was also a more somber “Justice for Harambe” petition that sought to hold the mother of the boy who fell into the enclosure responsible for the gorilla’s death. The county prosecutor determined there was no cause for charges.
Fiona swallowed the hat about 12 days ago after a zoo visitor tossed it in the air, it struck a ceiling fan and deflected into the hippo enclosure through a small opening above the viewing windows. It was an accident, a zoo spokesperson said.
She was not the first zoo animal to die from eating a non-food item that found its way into a pen. Zoos around the world have been warning for years about the dangers posed by objects that are tossed or blown into animal habitats.
Two years ago, a rare antelope choked to death after eating the plastic lid from a squeezable fruit pouch at a zoo in Tennessee. A polar bear at a German zoo died in 2014 after swallowing a jacket dropped into his enclosure by a visitor.
But the accidental nature of Fiona’s death hasn’t dampened the despair.
“The two saddest days in all my time here in Cincinnati come from the Zoo,” Facebook user Marianne King posted Thursday. The first was Harambe’s death and the second was Fiona’s, she said.
Joanne Prater, who lives in the Cincinnati suburb of Loveland, was attending a high school fundraiser Thursday evening and said every person she spoke to talked about how sad they were about Fiona’s death and compared it to Harambe’s.
“They are tokens of Cincinnati. You can’t say Fiona or Harambe without everybody knowing who that is here in Cincinnati,” she said. “I guess both of their deaths could have been prevented, but unfortunately accidents do happen.”

sources.news_title: Cincinnati Zoo's famed Fiona the hippo dies days after eating a visitor's hat
sources.text:
CINCINNATI | Fiona, the hippo whose premature birth and fight for survival at the Cincinnati Zoo turned her into a global sensation nearly a decade ago, died Thursday from complications after swallowing a knit hat that was accidentally flung into her enclosure. She was 9 years old.
“It is with extreme sadness that we share with you the devastating news that Fiona did not make it after multiple attempts from our amazing vets and keeper team to help her through what ended up being a medical emergency,” the zoo said in a statement.
The zoo said Monday that it was providing Fiona with round-the-clock care after she swallowed the hat more than a week ago. Specialists had advised that surgery wasn’t an option for a full-grown hippo like Fiona.
Before she died, veterinarians had been keeping Fiona hydrated, giving her treats and monitoring her every move, the zoo said. They borrowed a vibration plate from a horse farm, encouraging her to stand on it several times a day in the hopes that the shaking would help move the hat through her digestive tract.
“Despite multiple attempts to move the hat out of her system, it was ultimately too much to overcome,” the zoo said.
Within an hour of the announcement, visitors began leaving flowers and cards by a hippo statue outside the zoo. “Forever our Fiona,” one note read.
Fans mourn Fiona
Fiona captivated people worldwide after her premature birth in 2017. Her presence was felt all around the zoo, which was scheduled to stay open late Thursday for the first night of its Festival of Lights.
Amy Haacke, a special educator from Dayton, said outside the Cincinnati Zoo that she’s been a “huge fan” of Fiona since she was born because she likes underdogs. Haacke said she uses the Fiona book series in her classroom and owns three Fiona shirts.
“We were coming here anyway, but it kind of means a lot to be here,” Haacke said Thursday. “We were here when she was first born and, I guess, now we’re here when she’s gone.”
Yolanda Gould, who works more than 80 miles (130 kilometers) away in Covington, said she and others in her office left early to travel to the zoo after learning about Fiona’s death. She said outside the zoo that she was feeling “a little devastated” after following Fiona since she was born.
Cincinnati Mayor Aftab Pureval said on social media that Fiona was “a symbol of perseverance and joy” in the city. Ohio Gov. Mike DeWine called her “a true icon.” The Cincinnati Bengals also expressed condolences, dubbing Fiona “the queen of the Queen City.”
In a joint post with U.S. Vice President JD Vance on Instagram, second lady Usha Vance shared a photo of one of their children face-to-face with Fiona through a glass wall of her enclosure. The family has a home in Cincinnati.
“We are so sad to hear the news about Fiona,” she said in the caption. “Our family loved visiting her at the Cincinnati Zoo.”
Fiona was under close care
Fiona swallowed the hat about 11 days ago after a zoo visitor tossed it in the air. A ceiling fan caught and deflected the hat into the hippo enclosure through a small opening above the area’s viewing windows.
It was an accident, zoo spokesperson Michelle Curley said.
Before Fiona died, Mike Wenninger, the zoo’s director of animal health, said veterinarians had sedated her twice to evaluate her condition.
An ultrasound on Tuesday showed some bunching of her intestines, Wenninger said. They also conducted a colonoscopy using a 9-foot (2.7-meter) scope but were unable to detect anything, he said.
The Association of Zoos and Aquariums, the accrediting body for facilities, said in a statement Thursday that the Cincinnati Zoo provided “extraordinary 24/7 care for Fiona throughout this heartbreaking event.”
Surgery would have been challenging
Surgery would have been a major logistical challenge — multiple incisions would have been needed during a very long surgery, as hippos are notoriously difficult to anesthetize and have thick skin, said Jack Kottwitz, assistant professor at Michigan State University’s College of Veterinary Medicine.
The hat and its blend of fibers posed a particular danger despite its relatively small size.
Experts said hippos have a multichambered stomach for digesting plants, and the system makes for a very large gastrointestinal tract through which anything would have to travel.
Jan Hawkins, doctor of veterinary medicine at North Carolina State University, said Fiona’s situation was difficult because it would have been hard to tell where in her body the hat was.
“You can’t do the normal imaging and things that you can do in some of the smaller animals, or even horses,” Hawkins said.
Zoos around the world have warned for years about the dangers posed by objects that are tossed or blown into animal habitats. Two years ago, a rare antelope choked to death after eating the plastic lid from a squeezable fruit pouch at a zoo in Tennessee. A polar bear at a German zoo died in 2014 after swallowing a jacket dropped into his enclosure by a visitor.
Fiona became a sensation after Harambe’s death
Fiona survived her first health scare when she was born six weeks premature. She weighed just 29 pounds (13.2 kilograms), which was less than the lowest recorded birth weight for her species at that time.
She was unable to nurse, so a zoo staffer hand-milked her mother. The zoo recorded her progress with photos and videos, while fans worldwide followed her progress online.
Her story marked an uplifting turn for the Cincinnati Zoo after months of backlash over the shooting of Harambe, the gorilla who became a pop culture phenomenon after he was killed because a child got into his enclosure.
The zoo’s hippo family expanded in 2022 with the birth of Fiona’s baby brother, Fritz.
Fiona’s father, Henry, was euthanized months after her birth as his health badly declined. He had lived 36 years, slightly beyond the average life expectancy for a Nile hippopotamus in captivity.
Associated Press reporters Sallee Ann Harrison in Cincinnati, Alexa St. John in Detroit, Hannah Schoenbaum in Salt Lake City and Josh Kelety in Phoenix contributed.

By yourNEWS Media Newsroom
Fiona, the Cincinnati Zoo’s widely recognized hippopotamus whose survival after a premature birth in 2017 attracted millions of followers worldwide, died Thursday, Nov. 19, after swallowing a visitor’s knit hat that accidentally entered her enclosure more than a week earlier.
The 9-year-old Nile hippopotamus died following extensive veterinary intervention, including medical examinations, a colonoscopy and efforts to move the foreign object through her digestive system. The Cincinnati Zoo & Botanical Garden confirmed her death Thursday, saying the animal care team had exhausted available treatment options.
“We are in shock at the moment,” Cincinnati Zoo Director Dave Jenike said. “We did not expect this outcome. She fought until she couldn’t anymore.”
The incident occurred approximately 11 days before Fiona’s death when a visitor tossed a knit hat into the air inside the zoo. The hat struck a ceiling fan and was propelled through a small opening above the viewing windows into the hippopotamus enclosure, where Fiona swallowed it.
Zoo spokesperson Michelle Curley described the incident as accidental, according to reporting by The Associated Press. Fiona initially showed no obvious symptoms, but her condition later deteriorated as the hat failed to pass through her digestive tract.
Veterinarians began monitoring Fiona continuously, providing hydration, nutritional support and additional examinations to assess whether the obstruction could be resolved without surgery. The zoo announced Monday that she was receiving around-the-clock medical attention.
Medical specialists determined that surgery would be exceptionally dangerous for a full-grown hippopotamus. The procedure would have required multiple incisions, prolonged anesthesia and intervention within an unusually large and complex digestive system.
Fiona weighed approximately 2,500 pounds, and her size complicated both diagnostic procedures and potential surgical treatment.
Zoo veterinarians sedated her twice to conduct examinations. An ultrasound performed Tuesday showed portions of her intestines bunching together, indicating that the digestive tract was attempting to move material through her system.
The veterinary team also performed a colonoscopy using a 9-foot-long scope, but the procedure did not locate the swallowed hat.
In an additional effort to encourage movement through her digestive tract, zoo personnel borrowed a vibration plate from a nearby horse farm. Fiona was encouraged to stand on the equipment several times daily in hopes that the vibrations would help the hat pass naturally.
Veterinarians continued monitoring her hydration, appetite and activity while administering supportive care. Despite those interventions, Fiona’s condition became critical.
“Despite multiple attempts to move the hat out of her system, it was ultimately too much to overcome,” the zoo said.
The animal care team performed additional emergency treatment Thursday, but Fiona did not recover.
“Our animal care team was heroic in their efforts to save her. They did everything possible, but her body couldn’t fight anymore,” Jenike said. “She was dearly loved by her Zoo family and countless others around the world. Her loss will be felt deeply by so many.”
Veterinary specialists explained that hippopotamuses possess multichambered stomachs adapted for digesting plant material, making the passage of foreign objects especially difficult. Their substantial body size and thick skin also complicate imaging, anesthesia and surgical procedures.
Jan Hawkins, a veterinary specialist at North Carolina State University, said identifying the precise location of the obstruction presented considerable challenges.
“You can’t do the normal imaging and things that you can do in some of the smaller animals, or even horses,” Hawkins said.
The Association of Zoos and Aquariums acknowledged the Cincinnati Zoo’s efforts, praising the continuous veterinary attention Fiona received during the medical emergency.
News of her death prompted an immediate response from visitors and supporters. Within an hour of the announcement, mourners began placing flowers, cards and messages beside a hippopotamus statue outside the zoo.
Cincinnati Mayor Aftab Pureval described Fiona as “a symbol of perseverance and joy,” while Ohio Gov. Mike DeWine called her “a true icon.” The Cincinnati Bengals referred to her as “the queen of the Queen City,” and the Cincinnati Reds also paid tribute.
Vice President JD Vance and second lady Usha Vance joined those expressing condolences. In an Instagram post featuring a photograph of one of their children looking at Fiona through the enclosure’s glass viewing area, Usha Vance recalled the family’s visits to the zoo.
“We are so sad to hear the news about Fiona,” she wrote. “Our family loved visiting her at the Cincinnati Zoo.”
Fiona became internationally known shortly after her birth on Jan. 24, 2017, when she arrived six weeks prematurely and weighed just 29 pounds, substantially below the previously recorded minimum birth weight for her species.
Initially too weak to stand or nurse, she required intensive veterinary care and assistance from zoo personnel, who hand-milked her mother to provide nourishment.
The zoo documented her recovery through photographs and videos, attracting an international audience that followed her development from a critically underweight newborn into a healthy adult hippopotamus.
Her survival helped establish Fiona as one of the Cincinnati Zoo’s most recognizable animals. Her story inspired children’s books, merchandise and extensive social media coverage, while drawing attention to hippopotamus conservation and veterinary care.
The zoo’s hippopotamus family expanded in 2022 with the birth of Fiona’s younger brother, Fritz. Her father, Henry, had been euthanized several months after Fiona’s birth because of declining health.
Fiona’s story also brought renewed public attention to the Cincinnati Zoo following the 2016 death of Harambe, a gorilla fatally shot after a child entered his enclosure.
Thane Maynard, the zoo’s executive board chair, reflected on Fiona’s influence and the unusually strong public connection she developed during her lifetime.
“Fiona was such a gift,” Maynard said. “I have never known an animal so beloved in all my life. From the day she was born, she was like lightning in a bottle. And, she will be remembered and beloved many years from now.”
Fiona would have celebrated her 10th birthday on Jan. 24, 2027.
Her death also underscores the dangers posed by foreign objects entering animal habitats, even when incidents are accidental. Similar cases have resulted in fatalities at other zoological facilities, including a rare antelope that choked on a plastic food pouch cap at a Tennessee zoo and a polar bear that died after swallowing a visitor’s jacket at a German zoo in 2014.
The Cincinnati Zoo has asked the public to respect the privacy of the veterinarians and animal care personnel who worked to save Fiona, acknowledging the emotional impact of her death on employees who had cared for her throughout her life.
The zoo said Fiona’s survival, public recognition and role in raising awareness about hippopotamuses would remain an important part of its history.

sources.news_title: Cincinnati sports teams pay tribute to Fiona the hippo
sources.text:
Cincinnati’s major professional sports teams paid tribute to Fiona the hippo after the Cincinnati Zoo announced her death on Thursday.
Fiona, a 9-year-old Nile hippopotamus, died from health complications after ingesting a child’s knit cap that entered her enclosure. A visitor tossed the hat into the air, a ceiling fan caught it, and it was propelled through a small opening above the viewing windows.
Zoo director Dave Jenike said the animal care team was heroic in its efforts to save her and did everything possible, but her body could not fight anymore. He added that she was dearly loved by her Zoo family and countless others around the world.
Born six weeks premature on January 24, 2017, weighing only 29 pounds, Fiona became the first known Nile hippo to be hand-raised in a zoo and required intensive around-the-clock care. She survived against steep odds, grew into a worldwide sensation, and became a lasting symbol of resilience for Cincinnati.
Her death at age 9, well short of the typical 40-to-50-year lifespan for hippos in captivity, has left the Queen City mourning one of its most cherished icons.

sources.text:
CINCINNATI — A hippo from Ohio that became a worldwide sensation has died after eating a knit hat thrown into her habitat. Fiona was 9 years old.
The Cincinnati Zoo said in a statement, “It is with extreme sadness that we share with you the devastating news that Fiona did not make it after multiple attempts from our amazing vets and keeper team to help her through what ended up being a medical emergency,” The Associated Press reported.
Necropsy findings
Update 1:57 p.m. ET, Nov. 20: A necropsy found the hat was in the middle of her small intestine and that caused her death, the AP reported.
The zoo said no supportive care could have saved her.
Original report: A zoo visitor had tossed the hat in the air, and a ceiling fan caught it and tossed it into the enclosure through a small opening above the viewing windows, WHIO reported. Zoo spokesperson Michelle Curley called it an accident.
She had swallowed the hat more than a week ago and was receiving around-the-clock care, while surgery, according to specialists, was not an option for a fully grown hippo.
Veterinarians had been keeping her hydrated and giving her treats, and even went as far as using a vibration plate from a horse farm to help move the hat through her digestive system.
“Despite multiple attempts to move the hat out of her system, it was ultimately too much to overcome,” the zoo said, according to the AP.
Tributes to the beloved hippo started cropping up shortly after news of her death spread, with zoo visitors leaving flowers and cards at a hippo statue outside the zoo.
Cincinnati Mayor Aftab Pureval called Fiona “a symbol of perseverance and joy” while Ohio Gov. Mike DeWine called her “a true icon.” The Cincinnati Bengals called her “the queen of the Queen City.” Governor-elect Amy Action called the hippo’s death a “terrible loss, WHIO reported.
Fiona had been born prematurely in 2017 and captured the world’s attention as she grew into an adult hippo. She weighed only 29 pounds, or about a third of the size of a normal baby hippo, and could not stand or nurse, the AP reported in 2018. Staff had to milk her mother and, with help from the Smithsonian’s National Zoo, developed a formula for her.
Fiona’s birth came after months of uproar after the killing of Harambe the gorilla after a child got into his enclosure, the AP said.

sources.news_title: Fiona the hippo, beloved star of the Cincinnati Zoo, passes away at age 9
sources.text:
We at CB promised to keep you updated on Fiona the hippo, who had been receiving round-the-clock medical treatment as she struggled to pass a knit hat she ate when it landed in her enclosure in a freak accident. This is not the update we wanted to share with you. Her Cincinnati Zoo caretakers broke the news Thursday afternoon that Fiona had succumbed to her ingestive injuries. Here is their post in full:
It is with extreme sadness that we share with you the devastating news that Fiona did not make it after multiple attempts from our amazing vets and keeper team to help her through what ended up being a medical emergency.
The vet staff tried everything they could to help her after she ingested a hat that ended up in her habitat by accident last week. Despite multiple attempts to move the hat out of her system, it was ultimately too much to overcome. The team performed necessary supportive care today in an attempt to save her, but it was not successful and she did not recover.
We know everyone in the community will be crushed by this news, as we all are.
Please keep her keepers and everyone who tried to help her in your thoughts as they try to navigate and come to terms with this shocking news. They are also, understandably, asking for space at this time.
[From Cincinnati Zoo’s Instagram]
Shortly thereafter, The New York Times penned a beautiful obituary for Fiona:
The internet delighted when she loafed, when she farted, when her tank of a body bobbed in the water, when she crashed a wedding proposal. It was Fionamania.
Words like “sassy, unbothered, unproblematic queen” were used to describe a baby hippopotamus without a blink of an eye. Fiona had her own Facebook reality show, and is the subject of a children’s book series.
The hashtag #teamfiona had been revived in recent days as the zoo updated her fans, young and old, on her progress.
As Fiona grew, the Cincinnati Zoo had an influx of visitors, eager to get a glimpse of the rotund cutie. A mural went up in her honor. Surveying local businesses, The Cincinnati Enquirer reported nearly $500,000 in sales of clothes, beer, cards and other items related to the animal ahead of her first birthday.
Fiona’s success encouraged other zoos to make a habit of announcing their smallest arrivals. She set the tone for other hippo celebrities, like Moo Deng, a pygmy hippo at a zoo south of Bangkok who became famous for her feisty interactions with zookeepers.
But the pure joy and resilience of Fiona gave everyone something to root for.
“Cincinnati loved Fiona from the very beginning, and so did we,” the children’s hospital said in a statement. “We were honored to be part of the team that helped care for her as a tiny premature hippo and then watched with the rest of the world as she grew, thrived and captured millions of hearts.”
…About two weeks ago, the unthinkable happened to one of the world’s most influential hippos. A child standing near Fiona’s enclosure tossed a knit hat into the air. The hat was whirled by a ceiling fan through a one-foot gap above the 12-foot-tall viewing window, and it landed in Fiona’s enclosure. An industry standard called protected contact means zoo staff will not enter the enclosures of certain animals when they are present.
Afterward, Fiona was behaving normally until earlier this week when her appetite started to decrease. Surgery isn’t an option for full-grown hippos, said Dr. Gabriella Flacke, a veterinarian at Zoo Miami who consulted on Fiona’s case. The weight of an adult hippo’s abdominal contents is so heavy that it would make healing very challenging, she said. And a hippos’s thick, protective skin would have also posed difficulties for recovery.
It’s not just that a hippo’s skin is too thick for surgery, but the oily texture makes it near impossible for bandages to stick. Plus putting hippos under anesthesia poses a lot of risks. I went on a deep dive on this before we even got the tragic news, wanting to know why they weren’t operating. Science aside, all that’s left is the grief. And holy hippo, this is a huge loss. Like I said in our previous coverage, it feels so wrong that a knit hat should be the undoing of a lady who defied the odds by surviving her six-week-premature birth. And for this to happen so close to her 10th birthday is another salt in the wound. Hippos can live to be 50 — Fiona had a lot of life left to live!
This is gonna hurt for a long time. The gates of the Cincinnati Zoo have become an impromptu memorial. Among the traditional stuffed animals, candles, and flowers, people are also bringing offerings of Fiona’s favorite foods: watermelon and pumpkin. SOB. Our condolences go out to Fiona’s mother Bibi and brother Fritz during this difficult time for their family.
Here’s to Fiona, the People’s Hippopotamus.
Fiona was a symbol of perseverance and joy in Cincinnati. She brought smiles to so many faces, from kids to parents to visitors from around the world.
Our city is heartbroken, but we couldn’t be more grateful that she was part of our lives and our community as a whole.

But they gave her all of their expertise and hearts and at the same time gave Fiona, and the world, a joyous 9 years. Fiona will always be in my heart.
May Fiona’s memory be for a blessing, for all who love her.

Humans suck. We’ve destroyed the environment, animal populations are collapsing everywhere, and then when an animal is in CAPTIVITY, this happens.
Not sure it’s a young child tho, heard it was a 12 or 13 yr old, which if true, should have absolutely known better. If u look at how high the ceiling fans are in that exhibit, it’s really not something a small child could have reached. Either way, there’s some elements of parental responsibility that should be looked at.

The part that upsets me the most is the story that they didn’t immediately tell someone – they just left in a hurry and other zoo visitors informed a zoo worker. I dont know if that’s true (sourcing on social media is not the best as we all know)…but if so that’s where I place the blame. They should have immediately found someone and reported the incident, not just…..left.

Fiona, the hippo who drew a worldwide following after surviving a premature birth, died Thursday after swallowing a visitor’s knit hat, the Cincinnati Zoo & Botanical Garden announced. She was 9.
Fiona swallowed the hat about 11 days before her death. A visitor tossed it into the air, and a ceiling fan sent it through a narrow opening above the exhibit’s viewing windows, according to The Independent. Zoo spokesperson Michelle Curley described the incident as accidental.
Veterinarians tried to help Fiona pass the hat and gave her supportive care again Thursday in an effort to save her, the zoo said.
“We are in shock at the moment,” Cincinnati Zoo Director Dave Jenike said in the zoo’s announcement. “We did not expect this outcome. She fought until she couldn’t anymore.”
Caregivers monitored Fiona around the clock and worked to keep her hydrated. They also borrowed a vibration platform from a horse farm and encouraged Fiona to stand on it, hoping the movement would help the hat pass, according to The Independent.
A colonoscopy using a 9-foot scope failed to locate the hat, and an ultrasound showed bunching in Fiona’s intestines, according to a zoo update covered by Cincinnati station FOX19. The zoo consulted specialists and concluded surgery was out of the question for a full-grown hippo.
Fiona arrived six weeks early in 2017 and was too small to stand or nurse from her mother, Bibi, according to the zoo’s account of her birth and recovery. Her keepers stepped in to feed her, keep her warm, and provide round-the-clock care.
The zoo shared regular updates on her progress for nearly two years, drawing fans worldwide as she grew. Fiona would have turned 10 in January.

Fiona ingested the hat on Nov. 8. Her care team worked around the clock in the days that followed, but she died despite their efforts.

Another visitor reflected on Fiona’s fight to survive and the impact of her death.

sources.news_title: Fiona's death gives parents a chance to teach kids about grief
sources.text:
- Fiona, a beloved hippo at Cincinnati Zoo, died after swallowing a hat.
- Her death offers parents a chance to teach children about grief and loss.
- Experts recommend clear language and open conversations to help children process emotions.
CINCINNATI — For many children, the death of Fiona, a beloved hippo at the Cincinnati Zoo, may be their first experience with losing an animal they have grown to love, even if they never met her in person.
Fiona, who was 9 years old, died Thursday from complications after swallowing a knit hat that was accidentally flung into her enclosure. Her death has sparked an outpouring of love from around the country for the Nile hippopotamus, with zoo visitors leaving flowers and cards by the statue outside the entrance.
Some parents whose children never even saw Fiona in person have been trying to keep the news from them. Samantha Haines, a mother in St. Petersburg, Florida, said she had been trying to shield her 10-year-old daughter, who loves hippos, because she "didn't want to worry her." But she told her daughter about Fiona's death Thursday.
Psychologists and grief specialists say when animals die, the experience can provide opportunities for parents to help children understand death and navigate difficult emotions, including grief.
Haines said they cried together for about 20 minutes before she told her daughter she could add her Fiona-themed ornaments to the Christmas tree in her room. When her daughter emerged, she was distracted by a book about dragons and didn't want to talk about the hippo.
"I think she just needs a distraction right now," Haines said. "We have recently experienced a heavy death in the family and have been on the roller coaster of the grieving process already."
Experts recommend using clear, age-appropriate language to explain that Fiona died and will not be coming back. Phrases such as "went to sleep" can confuse or frighten younger children.
Caregivers also do not need to have every answer. Acknowledging uncertainty and making space for questions can help children feel comfortable expressing their emotions.
Parents can also acknowledge their children's feelings and share their own sadness with them. Experts say there is no single right way to grieve, and children may need time and repeated conversations to process the loss.
"People are so averse to talking about death and grief, but it is the one thing that is guaranteed: We are all going to die. We need to be open to talking about that," Deirdra Flavin, CEO of the National Alliance for Children's Grief, previously told the Associated Press.
Kaitlyn Hermsen, a mother of four in Oconomowoc, Wisconsin, says her 8-year-old daughter would visit zoos to see hippos, and became obsessed with Fiona's story, especially because she and the beloved animal were close in age.
"Her love for hippos is so big that we traveled all the way from Wisconsin to Cincinnati to visit her," Hermsen said.
She said telling her daughter about Fiona's death was heartbreaking.
"Through the sadness, she found comfort in imagining Fiona in heaven with our dog, Loki, and her favorite cow, Betsy."
Comments flooded a Facebook fan page for Fiona, with people expressing a mix of sadness and frustration. Some urged others not to direct their anger at the family of the visitor whose hat landed in Fiona's enclosure, while others shared happy memories of visiting her.
Remembering Fiona through drawings, photographs, favorite videos or stories about her life can also provide comfort and a sense of closure. Such activities can help children celebrate the joy Fiona brought to others while beginning to understand that death is a permanent but natural part of life.

sources.news_title: The Nurses Who Saved Baby Fiona Went Back to Treating Premature Babies. Then Parents in the NICU Started Saying the Hippo's Name
sources.text:
Quick Take
- Their first IV lasted barely half an hour. What did the nurses try next?
- No hippo formula existed. The zoo's workaround involved a surprising lab.
- A zoo employee's memory from a year earlier led keepers to the one team that could help.
- Back on the hospital floor, one hippo's name started echoing among NICU parents. Find out what they were saying and why.
Darcy Doellman and Blake Gustafson had spent decades on the Vascular Access Team at Cincinnati Children’s, a group of IV nurses that often works with premature babies. In February 2017, they packed their supplies and ultrasound equipment and drove to the Cincinnati Zoo. “Driving over, we both paused and looked at each other and thought: Wait, we are dealing with a hippo! Reality set in,” Doellman told the hospital’s Inspire magazine in 2022.
Their patient was Fiona, the Nile hippo born six weeks premature who died this week at age 9. Gustafson recalled finding her on a concrete floor in a cinder block room, pale and on oxygen.
Their first line lasted about 30 minutes before the vein blew, WVXU reported. Gustafson then used ultrasound to set a longer catheter in a deep vein in Fiona’s leg and sutured it in place.
“Five bags of fluid later, Fiona is showing signs of recovery,” Christina Gorsuch, the zoo’s curator of mammals, said at the time. Doellman said the zoo team kept the catheter in for five days.
Back at the hospital, parents in the NICU started saying the hippo’s name. “In our NICU, so many of those parents say, ‘If Fiona can fight, I can fight,'” Gustafson said.
Why was a 29-pound hippo in such danger?
Fiona was born Jan. 24, 2017, at 29 pounds, about 25 pounds under the lowest birth weight on record for her species, according to the zoo. Hippo calves normally weigh 55 to 120 pounds. She could not stand or nurse on her own.
Wendy Rice, who chronicled Fiona’s care on the Cincinnati Zoo’s blog, wrote that body temperature was one of the first problems. Getting too cold would be fatal, so the team aimed for 97 to 100 degrees Fahrenheit. Wild hippos spend up to 16 hours a day in water, but Fiona was not yet strong enough to stay in a pool for long stretches.
What did keepers do?
Keepers turned a room above the hippo building’s boiler into a nursery that held air temperatures up to 90 degrees. It sat close enough to her parents, Bibi and Henry, that Fiona could hear and smell them. The care team rubbed diluted baby lotion over her body every hour to keep her skin from drying and cracking.
No hippo formula existed and Bibi couldn’t produce enough milk, so the zoo sent some of her milk to the National Zoo’s milk repository for analysis and built a formula to match.
Why couldn’t she nurse like a normal calf?
A hippo calf can nurse underwater: its ears fold and nostrils close automatically, and it surfaces to breathe about every 30 seconds, according to the San Diego Zoo Wildlife Alliance.
Fiona was at first too weak to nurse and took every meal through a stomach tube, Rice wrote. She moved to a bottle, then started teething, which most hippos don’t do until several months after birth. Within 72 hours she had all but stopped nursing, and she grew dehydrated and lethargic, with blood work showing her kidneys were affected.
That is when the zoo called the nurses. A zoo employee remembered a Vascular Access Team nurse using ultrasound to start an IV on the employee’s own child the year before Fiona’s birth, Doellman said, and that memory led the zoo to the team.
How did she grow up?
By July 11, 2017, Fiona weighed almost 375 pounds and swam with both Bibi and Henry for the first time, WVXU reported. Weeks earlier, on her first trip outside with her mother, Bibi tried to keep her in the shallow end of the pool and gave up, Rice wrote.
Around her first birthday she weighed 650 pounds, NPR reported. Twenty-seven million people had watched The Fiona Show on Facebook, and hundreds of children born premature had written to tell her: “I made it, and you will, too.” She reached 2,000 pounds in July 2022, according to TODAY.
What did the nurses carry with them?
Doellman said the two nurses spent an hour and a half with Fiona and checked on her every day afterward. “I have every book, stuffed animal, calendar and ornament there is, so I definitely follow her,” Gustafson said. She also said it’s “amazing to see how many people have named their kids Fiona”.
How did Fiona die?
Fiona swallowed a visitor’s knit cap that landed in her habitat by accident on Nov. 8, the Cincinnati Zoo said. She died Nov. 19 after her care team worked around the clock to save her.
“We did not expect this outcome. She fought until she couldn’t anymore,” zoo director Dave Jenike said. She is survived by Bibi and her half-brother, Fritz.

sources.news_title: Fiona the Hippo Died After Eating a Hat. But How Does a Hat Kill a Hippo?
sources.text:
Fiona, the Cincinnati Zoo’s famous hippo who charmed observers around the world, tragically died on Thursday due to medical complications after ingesting a knit hat that mistakenly entered her enclosure last week, according to zoo officials. Fiona was just nine years old when she died.
According to zoo officials, the hat that caused her death entered her enclosure after a child tossed it into the air. The hat reportedly collided with a ceiling fan, which then launched the hat through a “one-foot gap above the 12-foot-tall viewing window.” A few days after eating the hat, her condition began to deteriorate.
For nonexperts, Fiona’s tragic death raises several questions: Why and how would a knit hat kill a hippo that weighs more than 2,500 pounds? Why wasn’t surgery possible for Fiona? And, for zookeepers, what was the range of treatment scenarios available?
Why Did Fiona Die?
Jan Hawkins, the head of the clinical science department at North Carolina State University’s College of Veterinary Medicine, tells WIRED that—with the caveat that we won’t officially know until doctors conduct a post-mortem analysis—Fiona’s death was likely due to one of a few downstream effects of the hat getting caught somewhere in her intestinal tract.
In a sense, an intestinal blockage in a hippo is like a car crash on an incredibly long one-lane highway. Hawkins said that, estimating, a hippo’s intestinal tract is likely over 100 feet long, with more than 70 feet in the small intestines alone. In humans, the lengths of the small and large intestines are a comparably diminutive 25 feet.
Hawkins says that in a healthy hippo, liquids can take as little as 12 hours to pass, and food takes two to three days. According to zoo officials, Fiona ate the hat on or about Sunday, November 8. Zoo officials claimed that Fiona was asymptomatic at first but began to lose her appetite after a few days. If the hat was going to come out, Hawkins says it likely would have happened within five days. So what happened?
One possibility, Hawkins says, is that when the hat got stuck, it caused a huge amount of swelling and pressure in her abdomen. That swelling could have led to her blood circulation being cut off and, eventually, to tissue death. After becoming green or black, Hawkins says, dead tissue is more likely to leak, and perhaps rupture, releasing the contents of the digestive tract into her blood. This can easily cause toxic shock.
In Fiona’s situation, this would mean that bacteria in her digestive tract died and released toxic molecules. If these toxins enter the bloodstream, Hawkins says, that would cause the organs to become more and more inflamed. Ultimately, this can lead to organ failure and death.
Another possibility is that, after the hat got stuck, Fiona’s intestines began to “twist on itself,” Hawkins says. This would be more likely if the hat, say, got pieces of food stuck inside of it, gradually becoming larger and heavier. Intestines are supposed to contract and move as they digest food. This means that if a heavy object gets stuck, the intestine can start to twist around it. In severe cases, this can cut off blood circulation. Eventually, this too can lead to tissue death. This initiates the chain of intestines leaking or rupturing, toxins entering the bloodstream, and organs becoming inflamed and eventually failing.
We don’t know exactly where the hat was in Fiona’s digestive tract. In a video the Cincinnati Zoo published to X on Tuesday, however, an unnamed staffer claimed that an ultrasound showed “some bunching of intestines.” They believed this meant that Fiona was “passing some things through her small intestine.”
If the hat was in Fiona’s small intestine, this would have meant that it passed through all three of her stomachs. (Hippos have three stomachs.) This could provide some hints about the type of hat that Fiona ate.
Hawkins says that in hippos, all three of their stomachs have the same basic components, but in different amounts. The first stomach has the largest amount of bacteria and protozoa, which help break down big pieces of food in the earliest part of digestion. The third has the highest amounts of enzymes and hydrochloric acid, which reduce food scraps into their smallest possible size before entering the small intestine.
“Let’s say it was a cotton hat or some sort of organic material, it’s possible that that could partially break down,” Hawkins tells WIRED. “Whereas if it had something that would not degrade—so a plastic, or polyester, or something like that—then obviously its character is not gonna break down at all.”
The effects of this, Hawkins says, would be even more severe if the hat were rigid or not collapsible in any way. “If it wouldn’t get scrunched down, like a hair scrunchie, then you could understand why it would get stuck,” Hawkins says. “Because it can’t change its character as much.”
All of this, Hawkins says, may have affected whether Fiona was able to pass the hat.
Why There Wasn’t a Surgery
According to the Cincinnati Zoo’s Tuesday video, conducting surgery to remove the hat would not be possible for Fiona. The zoo said that a combination of specialists—including “veterinarian human specialists,” zoo employees, and “other experts”—came to the conclusion that surgery wasn’t the best option and that the “best chance for success with Fiona would be if she can pass this on her own.”
Rebecca Lewison, a San Diego State University biology professor and cochair of the Hippo Specialist Group of the International Union for Conservation of Nature, tells WIRED that when it comes to hippo surgery, a major challenge is their “unpredictable and irregular responses to sedation and anesthesia.”
“It is very risky for [hippos], and they can die from the standard medication used on other large animals, like elephants and rhinos, for reasons we don’t well understand,” Lewison tells WIRED.
There are also some inherent challenges to administering anesthesia to an animal as large as Fiona. When a human or animal goes under anesthesia, they need to be put on a ventilator that artificially breathes for them. An animal that weighs more than 2,500 pounds, Hawkins says, requires a ventilator of a much different scale than what humans need for general surgery.
Fiona was placed under anesthesia to conduct bloodwork, according to the Cincinnati Zoo’s Tuesday video. But Hawkins says that the amount of anesthesia required for bloodwork is much smaller than what would be required for a major surgery, like removing a foreign object from her intestines. For Fiona, the increased amount of anesthesia alone increases the risk of the surgery.
Another fact to consider, Hawkins says, is the position the zoo would feasibly be able to place her in while conducting surgery. If a human is in surgery, they may be placed on their back, on their stomach, on their side, or in a variety of other positions. With animals like hippos, Hawkins says, this gets more complicated.
“You would have to have a hoist, a forklift or something, to pick them up to put them on either a pad or on a table,” Hawkins says. And if a zoo doesn’t have a table that’s big enough, the animal may have to go on the floor.
But Hawkins says that even at perfectly resourced zoos, there are other risks for hippos. In order to perform a major surgery, an animal as large as Fiona would have to have a huge amount of anesthesia, putting her unconscious and in the same position for a long period of time. She would have her entire body weight putting pressure on the parts of her body that can’t move. This would limit her body’s ability to circulate oxygen—even with the help of a great ventilator.
If an animal is unhealthy, Hawkins says, the risks are even greater. In its Tuesday video, the Cincinnati Zoo said that when it recently ran some tests on Fiona, it found that she was dehydrated. This means that her body was already working extra hard to circulate blood not only to the blockage but also through the rest of her body.
Animal caretakers in this position, Hawkins says, face incredibly difficult choices.
What Else Could They Do?
With surgery ruled out, the Cincinnati Zoo claims to have used a variety of other methods to help Fiona. In the Tuesday video, the zoo claimed that her early bloodwork did not raise any red flags. Zookeepers then conducted an ultrasound and administered rectal fluids, an enema, and medication, including some to help with vomiting and nausea. Later, the Tuesday video says, the zoo “borrowed a nine-foot scope from Columbus Zoo” with the goal of getting “far enough up to reach something.”
On Wednesday, Cincinnati Zoo said in a post that it had borrowed a “vibration plate” from a local horse farm with the hope that it would “encourage movement through her digestive tract and help the object pass.”
The zoo said that it also encouraged Fiona to eat and offered her some of her favorite foods.
“Her care team even offered her a sniff of coffee, a scent she always has really liked, and they were happy to see her respond,” the zoo said Wednesday evening.
But in the end, it wasn’t enough, but not for lack of trying. Hawkins says it sounds like “they threw everything at her but the kitchen sink.”
Hawkins adds, “I think they did not want to leave a stone unturned.”

Fiona’s death gives parents a chance to teach kids about grief — and life
A beloved 9-year-old hippo at the Cincinnati Zoo has died after swallowing a knit hat
For many children, the death of Fiona, a beloved hippo at the Cincinnati Zoo, may be their first experience with losing an animal they have grown to love, even if they never met her in person.
Fiona, who was 9-years-old, died Thursday from complications after swallowing a knit hat that was accidentally flung into her enclosure. Her death has sparked an outpouring of love from around the country for the Nile hippopotamus, with zoo visitors leaving flowers and cards by the statue outside the entrance.
Samantha Haines, a mother in St. Petersburg, Florida, said she initially kept the news that Fiona had swallowed a hat from her 10-year-old daughter, who loves hippos, because she “didn’t want to worry her.” But she told her daughter about Fiona’s death Thursday.
Psychologists and grief specialists say when animals die, the experience can provide opportunities for parents to help children understand death and navigate difficult emotions, including grief.
Haines said they cried together for about 20 minutes before she told her daughter she could add her Fiona-themed ornaments to the Christmas tree in her room. When her daughter emerged, she was distracted by a book about dragons and didn’t want to talk about the hippo.
“I think she just needs a distraction right now,” Haines said. “We have recently experienced a heavy death in the family and have been on the roller coaster of the grieving process already.”
Experts recommend using clear, age-appropriate language to explain that Fiona died and will not be coming back. Phrases such as “went to sleep” can confuse or frighten younger children.
Caregivers also do not need to have every answer. Acknowledging uncertainty and making space for questions can help children feel comfortable expressing their emotions.
Parents can also acknowledge their children’s feelings and share their own sadness with them. Experts say there is no single right way to grieve, and children may need time and repeated conversations to process the loss.
“People are so averse to talking about death and grief, but it is the one thing that is guaranteed: We are all going to die. We need to be open to talking about that,” Deirdra Flavin, CEO of the National Alliance for Children’s Grief, previously told The Associated Press.
Kaitlyn Hermsen, a mother of four in Oconomowoc, Wisconsin, says her 8-year-old daughter would visit zoos to see hippos, and became obsessed with Fiona’s story, especially because she and the beloved animal were close in age.
“Her love for hippos is so big that we traveled all the way from Wisconsin to Cincinnati to visit her,” Hermsen said.
She said telling her daughter about Fiona’s death was heartbreaking.
“Through the sadness, she found comfort in imagining Fiona in heaven with our dog, Loki, and her favorite cow, Betsy.”
Comments flooded a Facebook fan page for Fiona, with people expressing a mix of sadness and frustration. Some urged others not to direct their anger at the family of the visitor whose hat landed in Fiona’s enclosure, while others shared happy memories of visiting her.
Remembering Fiona through drawings, photographs, favorite videos or stories about her life can also provide comfort and a sense of closure. Such activities can help children celebrate the joy Fiona brought to others while beginning to understand that death is a permanent but natural part of life.
