I have far more merch dedicated to a hippo in Cincinnati than anyone who doesn’t live in Cincinnati, and hasn’t even met said hippo, should. But when Fiona was born at the Cincinnati Zoo in January 2017, six weeks premature, her viral story became everyone’s, as she beat all conceivable odds to survive and, later, thrive as the zoo’s chomping, farting mascot. She grew into an international superstar, a symbol of hope and resilience whose death was always going to be inconceivable. Somehow, it’s so much worse.
Fiona died on Thursday after ingesting a knitted hat that had accidentally blown into her enclosure. Due to their size and other factors, hippos cannot undergo surgery. Just as they did during her entry into this world, the members of Fiona’s care team worked around the clock to support her, calling on experts in all species to lend their insight. The hope, the Cincinnati Zoo shared, was that with the help of fluids, and even an equine vibration plate, she could pass the hat on her own. This time, however, Fiona did not pull through. “Despite multiple attempts to move the hat out of her system, it was ultimately too much to overcome,” the zoo posted in a statement on Instagram. “The team performed necessary supportive care today in an attempt to save her, but it was not successful and she did not recover.”

On any given day, she was the main attraction for many of the zoo’s patrons, drawing in crowds of admirers even as she transformed from a small, rubbery mushroom into 2,500 pounds of pure beast. Somehow, her playful self always shone through, be it in the videos of her pirouetting across the water of Hippo Cove or making her Super Bowl winner predictions. I myself have a Fiona the Hippo Hat, a Fiona the Hippo T-shirt, and a Fiona the Hippo children’s book (I do not have children). The whole World fell in love.

A zoo spokesperson said that a hat was tossed into the air in front of Fiona’s habitat and got caught in a ceiling fan that “catapulted” the hat through the one foot gap above the viewing windows leading into her enclosure. The spokesperson also said “We probably couldn’t make that happen again if we tried. It was clearly an accident.” Later, Cincinnati Zoo clarified that Fiona had swallowed a knit hat on November 8, and that her care team was “cautiously optimistic” that she would pass it and make a full recovery.
On November 17, Fiona was sedated for a second time to evaluate her condition. Fiona was 9 years old.

Fiona the hippo, whose premature birth and survival at the Cincinnati Zoo drew an international following, died November 19 after efforts to help her pass a hat she had swallowed were unsuccessful, the zoo announced. She was 9, two months short of her tenth birthday.
In its announcement Thursday, the Cincinnati Zoo & Botanical Garden said veterinary staff had made repeated attempts to move the object through her system. Supportive care provided that day did not save her, the zoo said.
Zoo director Dave Jenike said the outcome had been unexpected and praised the animal-care team’s efforts. Thane Maynard, executive chair of the zoo’s board, described the depth of the public’s attachment to Fiona. The zoo asked that the people who had cared for her be given space.
A hat enters Hippo Cove
The Associated Press reported that Fiona swallowed the knit hat on November 8. Zoo spokesperson Michelle Curley said a visitor tossed it into the air and a ceiling fan sent it through an opening above the viewing windows into the enclosure. Curley described the incident as an accident.
The zoo publicly described the treatment effort on Monday, November 16. In an earlier AP report, staff said they were watching Fiona and working to help her pass the cap. The zoo’s statement at that stage expressed cautious optimism that she would recover.
Veterinarians tried fluids, a scope and vibration
A November 18 report by Cincinnati public-radio station WVXU documented the care preceding her death. Fiona initially showed no symptoms, according to the zoo, but her appetite diminished after several days. Staff administered fluids and medication, ran blood tests and offered foods she liked.
Mike Wenninger, the zoo’s director of animal health, said Fiona was sedated again Tuesday for further evaluation. An ultrasound showed bunching in her intestines. The team also performed a colonoscopy with a nine-foot scope borrowed from the Columbus Zoo, whose technician helped set up the equipment.
On Wednesday, keepers had Fiona stand on a vibration plate borrowed from a local horse farm. The zoo hoped the movement would help the object pass through her digestive tract. She also responded when offered the smell of coffee, a scent her keepers said she liked.
Wenninger said consultations with veterinary and human specialists had ruled out surgery for the full-grown hippo. The care team’s approach was to help her pass the object herself. Fiona remained off exhibit during treatment and was monitored around the clock.
A 29-pound newborn who needed constant care
Fiona was born January 24, 2017, six weeks before her expected March arrival. In its announcement of her name, the zoo said she weighed 29 pounds, about 25 pounds below the lowest previously recorded birth weight for the species. It listed a normal birth-weight range of 55 to 120 pounds.
She was too weak to stand and nurse from her mother, Bibi, who was 17 at the time. Staff provided critical care and kept Fiona near Bibi and her father, Henry, so the animals could hear and smell one another.
Christina Gorsuch, then the zoo’s curator of mammals, said the calf still needed to learn to nurse, walk and swim before she could rejoin her mother. The zoo said the name Fiona meant fair. Its early updates appeared on the zoo’s website and Facebook page.
The naming announcement also recorded a scientific milestone from before Fiona’s birth. Zoo researchers had obtained what the institution described as the first ultrasound image of a Nile hippo fetus, confirming Bibi’s pregnancy earlier that January.
Her story reaches children and local businesses
By November 2017, Fiona was the subject of a board book for very young readers. The zoo’s announcement of “Fiona’s Feelings” described photographs showing the hippo with expressions intended to help children recognize emotions. Its author was pediatrician John Hutton, owner of Blue Manatee Press.
Hutton said the book was aimed at children from birth to age 3. Copies were donated to infants in the newborn intensive-care unit at Cincinnati Children’s Hospital, recognizing both Fiona’s premature birth and hospital staff members’ assistance with her early care.
The zoo said a portion of the book’s proceeds would support it. The original announcement listed local bookstores, the hospital gift shop and zoo shops as sellers, with national distribution planned for early 2018.
As Fiona approached her second birthday, the zoo’s January 2019 retrospective recorded a more physical milestone: she had reached 1,000 pounds. A thousand fans had participated in the Fiona 1K Walk the previous month, despite rain.
Birthday celebrations extended to Cincinnati businesses. Graeter’s offered Chunky Chunky Hippo ice cream, Listermann Brewing reissued Fiona-themed beers, and Cincy Shirts offered temporary tattoos with Fiona merchandise. The zoo planned to share her second-birthday festivities on Facebook Live because cold weather would keep her indoors.
On her eighth birthday, January 24, 2025, the zoo announced that its Facebook account had reached 5 million followers. It attributed part of its online following to Fiona’s survival story.
Marketing manager Amy LaBarbara said staff had posted about Fiona every day during her first year. When they tried to reduce that frequency, followers objected and the daily updates continued. By 2025, the zoo said it no longer posted daily about her, while videos and posts featuring Fiona and her brother Fritz still attracted millions of views and likes.
That January 2025 announcement put the zoo’s audience across its social platforms at almost 9 million. The platforms included Facebook, TikTok, Instagram, X, YouTube and LinkedIn. The figure covered the institution’s accounts, rather than a separate account belonging to Fiona.
Fritz joins the family
Fiona’s younger brother was born August 3, 2022. His naming became another public event: the zoo received 90,000 suggestions from every U.S. state and more than 60 countries. Keepers narrowed the choices to Ferguson and Fritz, then invited people to vote.
In its August 15 announcement, the zoo said 223,542 votes had been cast, with 125,183 favoring Fritz. At that point, the calf and Bibi were bonding indoors while staff prepared for introductions to the habitat and other hippos. Keepers continued to publish updates across the zoo’s social-media channels.
A species ambassador and a water-dependent habitat
The zoo also used Fiona’s popularity to explain how hippos live. Its 2022 World Hippo Day accountdescribed animals that graze on land at night and depend on freshwater habitats. It said hippos in human care commonly live 40 to 50 years.
In the 2019 birthday announcement, the zoo described Fiona as an ambassador for her species and warned that habitat degradation, drought and poaching were reducing wild hippo populations. It also described the risk of conflict with people and livestock when animals travel farther to find food or water.
At Hippo Cove, the zoo described a system that recycled the exhibit’s 70,000 gallons of water. Filtration removed waste, straw and food debris, while tilapia consumed some debris before it reached the filters. A 400,000-gallon rainwater cistern beneath the African savanna exhibit supplied treated water for the habitat and other zoo uses.
The same account described a conveyor that removed larger particles from the water for composting, followed by sand filters for smaller debris. The zoo presented its water-recycling system as part of its conservation education about freshwater-dependent wildlife.
Broader research has examined how environmental changes affect mammals. FINCHANNEL’s April 2021 coverage of an Oxford-led review described major gaps in studies of climate risks to mammal populations, especially in vulnerable regions. The review found research covering 87 species; that was a historical research count.

The zoo said attempts to help Fiona pass a hat she had accidentally ingested were unsuccessful, and she did not recover despite supportive care.

(Cincinnati) — Fiona, the Cincinnati Zoo & Botanical Garden’s world-famous Nile hippopotamus, died Thursday at age 9. She suffered complications after swallowing a knit hat that accidentally entered her enclosure 11 days earlier.
The zoo announced her death on Facebook at 3:44 p.m. “It is with extreme sadness that we share with you the devastating news that Fiona did not make it after multiple attempts from our amazing vets and keeper team to help her through what ended up being a medical emergency,” the zoo said. Staff performed supportive care Thursday, but she did not recover.
Zoo director Dave Jenike said in a news release: “We are in shock at the moment. We did not expect this outcome. She fought until she couldn’t anymore.”
The trouble began Sunday, Nov. 8. A child’s knit hat was tossed into the air in front of Fiona’s habitat, Hippo Cove. A ceiling fan caught it and sent it through a one-foot gap above the 12-foot viewing windows. Fiona swallowed a significant portion of it.
A zoo spokesperson called it a freak accident. “We probably couldn’t make that happen again if we tried. It was clearly an accident,” the spokesperson said.
On Monday, Nov. 16, the zoo announced that Fiona had swallowed an object and was off exhibit and being monitored around the clock. Her care team said it was cautiously optimistic she would pass it. Veterinarians sedated her twice to evaluate her, and an ultrasound Tuesday showed bunching of her intestines, a sign she was still trying to pass the obstruction.
The team performed a colonoscopy with a 9-foot scope but did not find the hat, according to Mike Wenninger, the zoo’s director of animal health. They also gave her a large enema, fluids, painkillers and other medications. On Wednesday, staff borrowed a vibration plate from a local horse farm and encouraged her to stand on it several times a day, hoping the shaking would help move things along. She also responded to a sniff of coffee, a scent she had always liked.
Specialists told the zoo that surgery is not an option for full-grown hippos.
Fiona was born Jan. 24, 2017, six weeks premature. She weighed just 29 pounds, well below the 55 to 120 pounds recorded for Nile hippo newborns at the time. She was the first Nile hippo born at the zoo in 53 years.
She could not stand or nurse, so keepers bottle-fed her milk taken from her mother, the first time a hippo had ever been milked, along with formula. When she became dehydrated, clinicians from Cincinnati Children’s Hospital helped place an IV catheter.
Her fight to survive made her a global social-media sensation in 2017, an uplifting story for the zoo months after the Harambe gorilla shooting. She went on to star in books, including “Saving Fiona” and “A Very Fiona Christmas,” and inspired a downtown Cincinnati mural. Her name came from the “Shrek” character, whose ears hers resembled.
Fiona’s mother, Bibi, her half-brother Fritz and Tucker, an adult male hippo, remain at the zoo. Her father, Henry, died in October 2017. She would have turned 10 on Jan. 24, 2027. The zoo asked the public to keep her keepers in their thoughts and to give them space.

Some leave work early to pay respects

“I think she’s taught us all to be resilient,” she added. “I’m feeling incredibly sad for us to lose her as a community, but also for all of the staff and everyone here that has just really poured their lives into helping her.”

Harambe: Another famous departed Cincinnati Zoo animal
The 17-year-old gorilla, who was shot and killed in May 2016 after a 3-year-old boy got into his enclosure, became an online cultural phenomenon following his death.
Remembrances began soberly, with a “Justice for Harambe” petition seeking to hold the boy’s mother responsible for his death. The county prosecutor determined there was no cause for charges.
Over time, Harambe showed up in tongue-in-cheek online petitions to rename the hometown Cincinnati Bengals, to add his face to Mount Rushmore and to put him on the dollar bill. He grew the angel wings and halo of a deity in social media memorials.
Harambe has also shown up regularly in satirical social media posts. “Never Forget,” read some posts accompanying the gorilla’s photo superimposed on the U.S. flag. He has also surfaced in comedians’ acts.
Harambe’s legacy has endured over the past decade. In May, the White House posted a photo of Harambe on social media, writing, “An icon that became part of internet history, American culture, and an entire generation’s timeline.”
Zoo visitors mourn the underdog
Amy Haacke, a special educator from Dayton, Ohio, said outside the Cincinnati Zoo on Thursday that she’s been a “huge fan” of Fiona since the hippo was born because she likes underdogs.
“We were coming here anyway, but it kind of means a lot to be here,” Haacke said. “We were here when she was first born and, I guess, now we’re here when she’s gone.”
Haacke said that she uses her Fiona the hippo books in her classroom and that she owns three Fiona shirts.

Zoos have options once a large animal dies
Jan Hawkins, doctor of veterinary medicine at North Carolina State University, said generally when zoo animals die, an autopsy will be conducted, with samples, biopsies or cultures taken to determine what happened. Typically, this process is done the same day as the animal’s death, or shortly after, as fresher remains can provide better answers, Hawkins said.
Afterwards, some will cremate the animal, some will render the animals for fertilizer and some will bury the animal depending on local regulations.
Disposal is sure to happen quickly given the difficulty of refrigerating an animal Fiona’s size.
The spirit of Fiona lives on
A woman who was leaving the Cincinnati Zoo with a bag from the gift shop gave a stuffed Fiona the hippo plush to a young boy who brought flowers for the memorial.
The woman did not wish to be interviewed by media.
Many visitors of all ages have brought flowers to the zoo as they pay their respects.
Fiona’s death can be an opportunity to teach kids about grief
For many children, Fiona’s death may be their first experience with losing an animal they have grown to love, even if they never met her in person. Psychologists and grief specialists say these moments can provide opportunities for parents to help children understand death and navigate difficult emotions.

Experts recommend using clear, age-appropriate language to explain that Fiona died and will not be coming back. Phrases such as “went to sleep” can confuse or frighten younger children.

Fiona’s birth — and improbable survival — was a public relations coup for the zoo. She was a source of hometown pride, decorating local bakery cookies and adorning T-shirts, and drew lines that snaked around the zoo.

Surgery would have been a major logistical challenge for many reasons, specialists said
Hippos have a digestive system that would make Fiona’s situation tricky, Jack Kottwitz, an assistant professor at Michigan State University’s College of Veterinary Medicine, said before her death was announced.
“They have a multichambered stomach for digesting plants — sort of like a cow — but they don’t regurgitate and chew cud like a cow does. Those multiple chambers, tissue folds, fluid, and digesting food easily ‘hide’ the hat, making removal with an endoscope from the stomach chambers very difficult,” Kottwitz said.

Fiona survived her first health scare when she was born six weeks premature in 2017. She weighed just 29 pounds (13.2 kilograms), which was less than the lowest recorded birth weight for her species at that time.

Cincinnati Zoo staff said in a statement on Friday that the hat that killed Fiona, the beloved hippo, was in an unreachable spot in her intestinal tract.
Zoo staff said a postmortem exam showed the hat was in the middle of Fiona's small intestine, 25 feet beyond her final stomach compartment and 50 feet from the end of her intestines. The zoo's director of animal health, Dr. Mike Wenninger, said upper and lower GI endoscopy were unable to reach the hat.
Fiona died after swallowing a hat that was accidentally dropped into her enclosure, the zoo confirmed in an email to Newsweek on Thursday.

“We are in shock at the moment,” said Cincinnati Zoo director Dave Jenike on Thursday. “We did not expect this outcome. She fought until she couldn’t anymore.”
A spokesperson said the zoo was "devastated to have to deliver the news" and that staff had "tried everything they could" to help Fiona, including using a vibration plate to help her pass the hat through her digestive tract. Fiona was not able to undergo surgery because of her size.
“The location and anatomy made laparoscopic removal impossible. No treatment aside from supportive care had any chance for success, and the necropsy confirmed that no amount of supportive care would have worked,” Dr. Wenninger said on Friday.
Staff provided supportive care, including fluids, for Fiona after blood work showed her body was shutting down, Dr. Wenninger said.
Fiona had swallowed the hat after a visitor threw it into the air and a fan catapulted it into Fiona's habitat by accident.
"By every account, this was a very unusual accident," said American Veterinary Medical Association President Dr. Jen Quammen in an email to Newsweek earlier on Thursday. "Still, it’s an important reminder that animals can be seriously harmed when they swallow things they shouldn’t, whether they’re pets at home, animals on the farm, residents of a zoo or animals in the wild."
In a statement shared with Newsweek after news of Fiona's passing Thursday, Quammen said that while the AVMA cannot speak to Fiona's case in particular, blockages can prevent food and fluids from moving through an animal's digestive tract and, in severe cases, damage the intestinal wall, compromise blood flow and cause infection.
Even with excellent veterinary care, she said these cases can be complicated, and as with Fiona, fatal.
"Fiona’s loss is a painful reminder of how important it is to keep potentially dangerous objects away from animals," Dr. Quammen said.
How Old Was Fiona?
Fiona gained national notoriety after she was born prematurely and the zoo documented her fight to survive. She appeared on The Today Show, in The New York Times, was the subject of books and was credited with bringing tourists to the city.
She would have been 10 years old in January, according to the zoo.
“Fiona was such a gift,” said Cincinnati Zoo Executive Chair of the Board Thane Maynard. “I have never known an animal so beloved in all my life. From the day she was born, she was like lightning in a bottle. And, she will be remembered and beloved many years from now.”
Fiona is survived by her hippo family, including Bibi, Tucker, and Fritz, who staff said are eating and behaving normally after Fiona's passing.
“It’s difficult to know how they’re feeling, but they appear to be their normal selves," said Christina Gorsuch, director of animal care.
The zoo shared a video of the hippos swimming and enjoying pumpkins in their habitat.
How Long Do Hippos Typically Live?
According to National Geographic, hippos can live up to 40 years in the wild and up to 50 years in captivity. However, habitat loss and the ivory trade have had a negative impact on their lifespan in the wild.
The animals have been classified as vulnerable on the IUCN's Red List, although most recent estimates suggest that the population has stabilized since considerable declines in the 1990s and early 2000s.
The IUCN estimated that there are between 115,000 and 130,000 hippos left in the wild.

Hippos have a complicated digestive system, with a multichambered stomach for digesting plants, Jack Kottwitz, an assistant professor at Michigan State University’s College of Veterinary Medicine, said before Fiona’s death was announced.
Surgery would have been a major logistical challenge for many reasons, he said.
In order to find the hat, multiple incisions would have been needed during a very long surgery, he said. But hippos are notoriously difficult to anesthetize and have skin over 2 inches (5 centimeters) thick in places.
Jan Hawkins, doctor of veterinary medicine at North Carolina State University, said Fiona’s situation was difficult because it would have been hard to tell exactly where the hat was.
“You just don’t know because you can’t do the normal imaging and things that you can do in some of the smaller animals, or even horses,” Hawkins said.
Other zoo animals have also died from eating foreign objects
Zoos around the world have warned for years about the dangers posed by objects that are tossed or blown into animal habitats.
Two years ago, a rare antelope choked to death after eating the plastic lid from a squeezable fruit pouch at a zoo in Tennessee. A polar bear at a German zoo died in 2014 after swallowing a jacket dropped into his enclosure by a visitor.
Fiona became a sensation after Harambe’s death
Fiona survived her first health scare when she was born six weeks premature. She weighed just 29 pounds (13.2 kilograms), which was less than the lowest recorded birth weight for her species at that time.
She was unable to nurse, so a zoo staffer hand-milked her mother. The zoo recorded her progress with photos and videos, while fans worldwide followed her progress online.
Her story marked an uplifting turn for the Cincinnati Zoo after months of backlash over the shooting of Harambe, the gorilla who became a pop culture phenomenon after he was killed because a child got into his enclosure.
The zoo’s hippo family expanded in 2022 with the birth of Fiona’s baby brother, Fritz.
Fiona’s father, Henry, was euthanized months after her birth as his health badly declined. He had lived 36 years, which was slightly beyond the average life expectancy for a Nile hippopotamus in captivity.

Surgery had not been an option for the more than 900kg animal, according to the Cincinnati Zoo, who had consulted with both "veterinary and human specialists".

They were joined by nurses from the nearby Cincinnati Children's Hospital, experts at finding veins and caring for tiny beings.

The #TeamFiona hashtag began filling up social media with official updates from the zoo and requests and well wishes from fans all over the world.

#TeamFiona became a full-on brand for Cincinnati Zoo, filling its shop with accompanying merchandise, from magnets to T-shirts. The city rallied behind their new four-legged mascot too, a local brewery creating a special beer in honor of the hippo and local clothing company Cincy Shirts making a special Fiona T-shirt, with proceeds going to the zoo.

Fiona the Hippo’s Death Reveals Extensive Zoo Safety Concerns
sources.text:
Fiona, a Nile hippopotamus kept at the Cincinnati Zoo in Ohio — initially made famous in 2017 by being the first Nile hippo born at the zoo in over 50 years and the first to be scanned in the womb using ultrasound — has died. Her premature birth at just 29 pounds and the intensive care she received that followed drew widespread attention, making her an internationally beloved animal. Tragically, Fiona’s death, confirmed as of November 19, 2026, has caused just as much — if not more — public interest.
Fiona died after ingesting a child’s knit hat, which was thrown into a ceiling fan by a young zoo visitor and ejected into her enclosure as a result. The zoo discussed Fiona undergoing surgery to remove the hat but, because hippos are notoriously difficult to sedate and often move while under the effects of anesthesia, the zoo ultimately deemed it too risky.
While much of the public blames the parents for failing to stop the hat from entering Fiona’s enclosure, it is unrealistic to expect that parents watch their children 100% of the time. Accidents happen. Especially with children. And zoos have demonstrated, time again, that their very design does not forgive visitor accidents or lapses in judgement, despite zoo census data from 2024 indicating that over one‑third of all U.S. zoo visitors are children, with some estimates suggesting that over 60 million children visit accredited U.S. zoos annually.
Accidents at Zoos Can Have Dire Consequences for Animals
Accidents happen at zoos every day, with some having more dire consequences than others. The most frequent causes of accidents that may have fatal outcomes — for the animals, the humans, or both — often occur due to visitors (intentionally or not) failing to read signs or heed instructions from zoo staff to avoid certain areas that would put them into dangerous proximity to potentially aggressive animals, enclosure breaches or damages that cause an animal to escape their habitat, open-air enclosures (which allow foreign objects to enter from visitors above, like in Fiona’s case), malfunctioning/unsafe exhibit doors/features, and any instances that allow for physical contact between human visitors and animals that could cause injuries due to bites or scratches. The one common thread between these potential accidents? Zoos are at fault for all of them.
It is the zoos’ responsibility to ensure that visitors remain safe on their premises, no matter how young, old, or noncompliant they may be. Wild animals are known to be dangerous and unpredictable, even when born and raised in captivity. The fact that dangerous incidents still occur almost every day at zoos across the country that jeopardize human and nonhuman animal lives confirms that, perhaps, no matter what safeguards are implemented, keeping wild animals in captivity is dangerous by nature and cannot ever be made entirely safe. Likely the best-known example that caused millions to question the safety of zoos was the shooting of Harambe the gorilla, which also occurred at the Cincinnati Zoo, ten years ago. Harambe was a 17‑year‑old western lowland gorilla who was shot and killed in May 2016 after a three‑year‑old boy fell into his enclosure.
Foreign Object Consumption is Not Rare at Zoos
Unfortunately, death or serious injury from foreign object consumption is not rare at zoos. Every year, there are several reports of captive animals at zoos consuming foreign objects thrown into their enclosures by zoo visitors. For example, in 2024, the Henry Doorly Zoo in Nebraska issued a warning to zoo visitors following the discovery of 70 coins in the stomach of a 36-year-old alligator named Thibodaux. A California sea lion at Moody Gardens, Texas, died in 2021 from ingesting a small plastic fish, which had been introduced to the enclosure as “enrichment.” In the same year, a young mountain lion who died at Cheyenne Mountain Zoo in Colorado was found to have an object that resembled rope or wire in their stomach.
In February 2022, Zoo Miami, Florida, revealed the variety of objects swallowed by their animals, including sunglasses, a water bottle, bottle caps, and children’s pacifiers after they had been dropped or thrown into animal enclosures. Similarly, Edinburgh Zoo in Scotland revealed a vet had carried out 22 surgeries within four years to remove foreign objects swallowed by their gentoo penguin colony, including socks, gloves, and batteries. In August 2022, Tallinn Zoo, Estonia, announced that their northern ground hornbill suffered a “painful death” after swallowing a coin, which resulted in the bird hemorrhaging from their beak.
Death by foreign object consumption is particularly prevalent in polar bears in captivity, potentially due to their largely opportunistic diet in the wild. A male polar bear named Umka died at a Russian zoo in 2021 after swallowing a toy ball thrown into his enclosure by a young visitor. In 2014, Anton, a 25-year-old male polar bear, died at the Wilhelma Zoo in Germany from severe intestinal injuries after swallowing a jacket or bag dropped into his enclosure by a visitor. In 2003, 14-year-old male bear, Andy, died at Hogle Zoo in Utah after swallowing a visitor’s glove that had found its way into his enclosure. And, in 1996, at Scotland’s Edinburgh Zoo, 20-year-old polar bear Barney reportedly died in agony after swallowing a toy that had either been accidentally dropped or deliberately thrown into the enclosure by a young visitor
Captivity for Human Entertainment Harms Animals
Wild animals are naturally curious, and living for decades in small, simplistic, unnatural, and largely unchanging environments causes animals to explore and consume potentially harmful objects that they typically would not encounter or have interest in in the wild. Like hippos, many of the animals kept at zoos cannot undergo invasive surgery without extreme risks. This begs the question: why do zoos continue to keep animals captive that cannot be saved from the negative effects of reasonable, routine accidents?
Help us spare the lives of future wild animals by choosing not to support zoos, aquariums, and any other facilities that hold animals captive just because they can. The animals did not agree to this lifestyle, so why should we support it? We implore you to honor Fiona’s memory, and all other wild animals who have lost their lives unnecessarily at zoos, by choosing not to fund their continuous exploitation of wild animals.
Keep Wildlife in the Wild,
